title: The Youngest VC in the Room
subtitle: A Chat With My 9-Year-Old About AI, Ads, and Why the Cybertruck Looks Like a Brick on Wheels
body_html:
I recently sat down with my daughter Quinn — almost 10, and deeply opinionated — to get her take on the AI industry. I paused her Taylor Swift playlist. She was not thrilled about it. What followed was one of the more insightful conversations I’ve had about product strategy in recent memory.

O: Let’s start with the basics: Quinn, what’s an entrepreneur?

Q: Someone who works in business. But like, more than regular people. They work a lot.

O: And you want to be one?

Q: Yeah. I like technology.

O: What technology impresses you?

Q: I learned about OpenAI and Anthropic from the Hard Fork podcast — it’s a technology podcast by Casey Newton and Kevin Roose from the New York Times. And that’s basically where I learned about all the AI companies.

O: What makes those companies good?

Q: They have a lot of people working on them, and they keep coming out with new models and updates. Like, ChatGPT is one thing, but then they made Sora. One time my babysitter saw something and thought it was real, and I had to explain it was a Sora video. That’s how good it is.

O: What about the Chinese AI companies? For example, there’s DeepSeek and Qwen 3.

Q: I like Qwen 3 because — well, that’s basically my name. They just replaced two letters. If it was actually called Quinn 3, it would probably be even better.

O: Is naming your product after potential users a good marketing strategy?

Q: Yeah.

(She said this with complete confidence and moved on.)

O: What’s your advice for OpenAI?

Q: You can use ads, but be careful. Make them related to what people are actually doing, so they get a little less annoyed. And don’t lock all the good stuff behind premium. Whatever you give to premium users, you should really just give to everyone. It works way better. Even if you still have ads — just don’t make them too… discreet?

(She meant intrusive. Or possibly both.)

O: What about Anthropic, which doesn’t have ads?

Q: They should look at Google. Google started by making everything very visible, and they kept adding things, and now they’re a really successful company. Anthropic and OpenAI should be looking at them.

O: Did you know Google basically did the research that made all these companies possible?

Q: Yeah. Google did all the work pretty much.

O: They published the paper on Transformer models.

Q: Yeah. And Safari is basically a copy of Chrome.

(It’s the other way around, but her point about derivative products stands.)

O: If you were starting a business as an almost-10-year-old, what would it be?

Q: I’d start something like AI, but with real safety measures. Like so, no one could look up how to make a nuclear bomb. All in on AI safety.

Also, I’d want to help make an alternative to YouTube for kids my age. Not YouTube Kids — that’s for little kids. I used it once and got bored really fast. And it was still pushing Ryan’s World, and that guy’s basically canceled now because his parents forced him into it, and now he’s a teenager still doing it because they make him. So, YouTube Kids is out.

O: What would you put on this hypothetical “YouTube Junior”?

Q: Brain-rot videos, obviously. Educational content — like channels that teach life lessons. Don’t judge a book by its cover; anyone can be anything, all that. And Mark Rober, because he teaches things without people realizing they’re learning. Some YouTubers teach history, and people don’t even notice. Also, research videos, because some people actually go on YouTube to learn things.

O: Do you know what product market fit means?

Q: No. Is it like a test run?

O: Exactly. It’s when you have so many customers you can barely keep up.

Q: Yeah. Because when I was brainstorming business ideas, I only came up with one, and it took forever. So I guess I don’t have product-market fit yet.

O: Any other business advice for young entrepreneurs?

Q: Don’t think you’re automatically going to get somewhere just because you have a brainstorm. It takes a really long time to come up with even one good idea. And once you have a product, you have to keep updating it. There was this Roblox creator who was huge and then stopped making good updates, and everyone left. Keep your brand fresh. OpenAI does a good job of that. With the ads thing, they need some work, but they’ll get there.

O: Any companies you want to shout out?

Q: SpaceX, because it’s very hard to get something into space. And Colossal Biosciences — I learned about them from a Mr. Beast video, which is honestly great PR. They’re working on bringing back extinct animals, and there’s also a biome project so that if the world ends, people will still be around in like a hundred billion years.

Also Neuralink, because there was someone on Mr. Beast whose arms are disabled and they made something so he can text using his brain. Neural… link?

O: That’s also Elon Musk.

Q: So that’s two out of three Elon Musk companies. Even though I don’t really like him that much, because of Teslas. Their self-driving is horrible. And the Cybertruck — there are just a lot of roasts about it. It literally looks like a brick on wheels.

O: You have a keen eye for product market fit.

Q: Yeah, and the Cybertruck was not a very good example of it.

Considering this was conducted in the car, and transcribed thereafter, on the way to skating…Not bad. To recap:

Quinn’s framework:

  • prioritize users over monetization,

  • ship updates constantly,

  • Name your product after your customers if possible, and

  • if you’re going to put something on wheels, make sure it doesn’t look like a brick.

She’s almost 10. The bar has been set.

The Frontier Psychiatrists is a newsletter about brain medicine, neuromodulation, and occasionally, what my kids think about AI strategy.

I can't emphasize enough how I want my readers to send this interview to either Casey Newton or Kevin (or both) so that the youngest listener to Hard Fork can get her due. If any of my readers are friends with the team there, share away!
